docs.title: 1.1 The Problem This Proposal Addresses
docs.text:
The EU's bioeconomy and nature market strategies — including the Carbon Removals and Carbon Farming (CRCF) Regulation (EU 2025/2358), the Nature Credits Roadmap, and the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) — require a fundamental transformation of how agricultural value is measured, distributed, and governed. Yet a critical gap persists: the methods and tools for quantifying the full, phase-resolved True Value of agricultural supply chains — including their environmental, social and climate costs and benefits — are not yet operational at the farm-to-market level.

Without this analytical infrastructure, policymakers cannot credibly balance bioeconomy incentives against food security safeguards. Farmers remain price-takers, unable to demonstrate the full value of their environmental stewardship. Markets for carbon credits, nature credits, and biodiversity offsets lack the supply chain grounding needed to prevent greenwashing, perverse incentives, and land-use conflicts.

docs.title: 1.2 The Opportunity
docs.text:
This proposal develops and validates the True Value Framework (TVF) — a quantitative, phase-resolved supply chain intelligence methodology — across three strategically chosen commodity systems:

  1. Shea (West Africa: Senegal, Burkina Faso, Mali, Ghana) — connecting the Great Green Wall (GGW) initiative and African women's cooperatives to EU cosmetics and food manufacturers
  2. Olive Oil (Spain, with Italy as the critical bulk-trade market) — the world's largest cooperative-based agricultural commodity, anchored in proven bioeconomy governance models
  3. Diversification commodities (Argentine soya/beef, Spanish cherries, other agri-food products) — to test framework scalability and cross-regional land-use conflict analysis

This selection is not arbitrary. These three systems together cover: (a) a North-South supply chain with deep Scope 3 GHG and biodiversity implications (Shea/GGW); (b) a mature EU cooperative sector with documented natural capital governance challenges (Olive Oil/Spain); and (c) a Global South commodity with high land-use conflict risk and AfCFTA relevance (Argentina/soya). Together they generate the comparative dataset required to produce generalizable, policy-applicable findings.

docs.title: 1.3 Why Now
docs.text:
• The EU Nature Credits Roadmap (2025) requires certification methodologies that do not yet exist at supply chain resolution
  • The CRCF Regulation (adopted November 2025) demands monitoring, reporting and verification tools for carbon farming — tools this project will develop and test
  • The EU Vision for Agriculture and Food explicitly calls for "fair income for farmers" and "resilient supply chains"
  • The GGW received $14 billion in pledges in 2021, yet only ~2% of restoration targets have been met; this project provides the value chain intelligence to unlock that capital
  • The deadline (17 September 2026) aligns with growing institutional urgency to operationalize these frameworks before the 2027 CAP review cycle

docs.title: Primary Objective
docs.text: To develop, validate and deploy a phase-resolved True Value Chain (TVC) analytical framework that enables farmers, cooperatives, policymakers and market operators to quantify, balance and communicate the full spectrum of bioeconomy, food security, climate and biodiversity impacts across agricultural supply chains.

docs.title: Specific Objectives
docs.text: # Objective Call Alignment SO1 Develop and validate natural capital accounting methods integrating economics, biodiversity and climate into agricultural supply chain accounts Scope: explore natural capital accounting SO2 Analyse existing and develop new innovative business models and value chains enabling fair value capture for primary producers Scope: develop new innovative business models SO3 Quantify Scope 1, 2 and 3 GHG emissions at phase resolution across the full shea, olive oil and diversification supply chains Scope: farm to macro level interdisciplinary research SO4 Assess land-use conflicts, food security risks and leakage effects across the three commodity systems Scope: land-use conflicts, food security risks SO5 Develop biomass supply-demand threshold models assessing tipping points where bioeconomy market prices alter production decisions Scope: biomass supply and demand threshold effects SO6 Produce evidence-based policy recommendations for the design of sustainable business models and value chains, addressing farmer income diversification under the CRCF and Nature Credits frameworks Scope: recommendations for policy and business model design SO7 Pilot the integration of TVF outputs into EU Economic Accounts for Agriculture and CRCF certification processes Scope: synergies with EAA framework and CRCF

docs.title: 3.1 Shea — West Africa to EU (Anchor Commodity)
docs.text:
Why Shea: Shea is simultaneously one of the most critical bioeconomy commodities linking the Great Green Wall (GGW) to EU markets and one of the most structurally opaque supply chains in global trade. An estimated 4–6 million women in West Africa depend on shea kernel collection and processing for their primary income. EU imports of shea butter feed the cosmetics industry (notably Unilever, L'Oréal, The Body Shop supply chains) and chocolate and confectionery manufacturers (as a cocoa butter substitute) — yet Scope 3 emissions and biodiversity impacts along this chain remain unmapped at the resolution needed for credible certification.

Scope and Geography: - Senegal, Burkina Faso, Mali, Ghana (production zones along the GGW corridor) - Processing and export hubs: Bobo-Dioulasso (BF), Dakar (SN), Accra (GH) - EU import/refining: France, Germany, Netherlands, Italy - End markets: EU cosmetics and chocolate manufacturers; retail sustainability commitments

True Value Framework Application: - Phase-resolved supply chain mapping (collection → kernel processing → butter production → export → refining → manufacturing → retail) - Full Scope 3 GHG accounting per phase - Biodiversity and ecosystem services valuation (parkland agroforestry, carbon sequestration, soil health) - Women's cooperative income diversification modelling (beyond food/feed to cosmetics, energy, organic fertiliser, carbon credits) - Land-use conflict assessment: shea parkland vs agricultural intensification vs mining concessions

Connection to Great Green Wall: The GGW represents the world's largest ecosystem restoration programme ($33 billion estimated total cost; $14 billion pledged by 2021). Shea agroforestry is a cornerstone of GGW land-use strategy in Senegal and Burkina Faso. This project directly addresses the documented gap: only ~2% of GGW national restoration targets achieved, partly due to absence of functioning value chain infrastructure linking restoration activities to market incentives. TVF supply chain analytics will provide the evidentiary foundation to unlock GGW-aligned carbon and nature credit mechanisms.

Key Data Partners: - National Union of Shea Producers (Burkina Faso) — 5,000 women's cooperatives - Nitidæ (France) — SHEA GETS GREENER project alumni - CIFOR-ICRAF — existing research on shea market integration - Impact Agri (contact: Jon White) — agribusiness supply chain analytics

docs.title: 3.2 Olive Oil — Spain (and Italy as Bulk Trade Market)
docs.text:
Why Olive Oil: Spain is the world's largest olive oil producer, with cooperatives accounting for approximately 60–70% of total production. The Andalusian olive sector is among the most intensively studied in EU bioeconomy governance research, and Spain has received specific OECD policy recommendations on cooperative-sector reform and natural capital integration. Italy is the critical bulk trade destination for Spanish olive oil — processing, re-labelling and distributing Spanish oil under Italian brands to global markets — creating a well-documented value appropriation asymmetry that the TVF methodology is directly designed to analyse.

Scope and Geography: - Spain: Andalusia (Jaén, Córdoba, Granada), Castilla-La Mancha — cooperative sector focus - Italy: Processing, import, and premium market re-distribution (bulk Spanish → branded Italian) - Argentina: Olive oil production expansion (Mendoza, San Juan, La Rioja) — emerging Global South competitor

True Value Framework Application: - Cooperative vs. non-cooperative value capture analysis - PDO (Protected Designation of Origin) and bioeconomy premium quantification - Olive mill waste (omurgha/pomace) as circular bioeconomy biomass — biorefineries, bioenergy, soil amendments - Land-use conflict analysis: water stress (olive is water-intensive in an increasingly arid Andalusia), olive monoculture vs. biodiversity corridors - Comparison of governance models: Spanish coops vs. Argentine private-sector supply chains - Benchmarking against OECD policy recommendations for Spain (cooperative sector reform, natural capital integration)

Key Data Partners: - Cooperativas Agro-alimentarias de España — national cooperative federation - Instituto de Investigación y Formación Agraria y Pesquera (IFAPA), Andalusia - ROBIN project (Horizon Europe-funded, Andalusia circular bioeconomy governance research) — complementarity partner - Università degli Studi di Bari Aldo Moro (Italy) — olive supply chain research

docs.title: 3.3 Diversification Commodities — Framework Scalability Testing
docs.text:
Argentine Soya and Beef: Argentina is the world's third-largest soya exporter and a major beef exporter to EU markets. Both commodities carry high land-use conflict risk (Chaco deforestation, Pampa degradation) and significant Scope 3 GHG exposure in EU supply chains. The EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) directly implicates Argentine soya and beef supply chains. The TVF methodology applied here will test framework scalability beyond African and European contexts and will generate the comparative dataset needed to assess land-use conflict dynamics across three distinct governance environments (Sahelian Africa, EU Mediterranean, South American pampas/subtropics).

Spanish Cherries and Other Horticultural Products: Spanish cherries (Extremadura, Jerte Valley) represent an intensively studied high-value horticultural commodity undergoing rapid market integration and bioeconomy transition. They serve as a domestically bounded EU test case for TVF application, with direct institutional linkages to Spanish agricultural research networks.

Other Agri-Food Commodities (to be confirmed with partners): The framework is designed to be modular. Additional commodities may be incorporated in consultation with consortium partners and the multi-actor panel, subject to data availability and alignment with project objectives.

docs.title: 4.1 Framework Overview
docs.text:
The True Value Framework (TVF) is a quantitative, phase-resolved supply chain intelligence methodology that models agricultural supply chains as structured physical and value systems, measuring at each phase:

  • Physical flows: mass, volume, transformation, custody transfer
  • Economic flows: costs, revenues, margins, value appropriation by actor type
  • Environmental accounts: GHG emissions (Scope 1, 2, 3), water, land, biodiversity impact
  • Social accounts: income distribution, labour conditions, gender equity, community impact
  • Governance structure: transparency, opacity classification, regulatory compliance

The methodological architecture follows the Negotiation–Definition–Contribution (N-D-C) triadic framework (Tholonic model), which structures each supply chain phase as a triadic system where: - N (Negotiation) = the stable, coherent operational state at that phase - D (Definition) = constraints, requirements and boundaries governing what the phase is - C (Contribution) = outputs, flows and connections governing what the phase does

Sustainability of any phase is measured by the D/C balance: when constraints and contributions are in equilibrium, the phase is most energy-efficient and resilient. Imbalance signals structural fragility, value leakage, or environmental risk.

This framework has been developed and validated on the gold supply chain (Phase 0–7, mineral origin to exchange-registered bullion) and is now being extended to agricultural commodity systems.

docs.title: 4.2 Phase Resolution
docs.text:
Each commodity supply chain is mapped to discrete phases, each defined by: - A physical state of the commodity - A transformation or custody change - A measurable output with units - An assigned transparency classification (High / Medium / Low / Opaque)

Example phase structure for Shea:

Phase Description Key Physical State Custody 0 Parkland ecological system Shea tree, standing biomass Community / commons 1 Kernel collection Dried kernel Women's cooperative / collector 2 Primary processing Shea butter (artisanal) Cooperative / aggregator 3 Export preparation Cleaned kernel or crude butter Aggregator / exporter 4 International transit Kernel or butter in bulk Exporter / shipping 5 Industrial refining Refined shea olein/stearin Refiner (EU) 6 Manufacturing integration Ingredient in product Manufacturer 7 Retail and end consumer Final product Retailer

docs.title: 4.3 Natural Capital Accounting Integration
docs.text:
The project will develop and test natural capital accounting methods aligned with: - SEEA (System of Environmental-Economic Accounting) — the UN framework for ecosystem accounts - EU Economic Accounts for Agriculture (EAA) framework — direct call requirement - IPBES biodiversity valuation protocols - CRCF Regulation certification methodology requirements — the project will contribute input to Delegated Acts expected in 2026

For each commodity and phase, a Natural Capital Account will be constructed containing: - Provisioning ecosystem services (food, fibre, fuel) - Regulating ecosystem services (carbon sequestration, water regulation, pollination) - Cultural ecosystem services (livelihood, heritage, gender empowerment) - Biodiversity metrics (species richness, habitat quality, connectivity)

docs.title: 4.4 Scope 3 GHG Accounting
docs.text: Full Scope 3 GHG emission accounting will be conducted for the shea supply chain as the primary pilot (with olive oil as secondary). This addresses a critical gap: cosmetics and food companies with Scope 3 disclosure obligations under CSRD (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive) lack supply chain-resolved emission factors for shea butter. The project will generate: - Per-phase GHG emission factors (kg CO₂e per kg commodity) - Attribution of emissions by supply chain actor type - Uncertainty ranges and transparency classification - Integration pathway into existing LCA databases (ecoinvent, etc.)

docs.title: 4.5 Biomass Threshold Modelling
docs.text: A core methodological innovation is the development of biomass supply-demand threshold models — quantitative assessments of the market price levels at which bioeconomy incentives (carbon credits, nature credits, bioenergy contracts) begin to divert agricultural biomass from food/feed to non-food uses, triggering food security risks. These threshold models will be calibrated separately for each commodity system and validated against historical market data.

docs.title: 4.6 Land-Use Conflict Assessment
docs.text: The project will apply a spatial land-use conflict index to each commodity system, assessing: - Direct competition between food production, bioeconomy crops, carbon forestry, and nature restoration - Leakage effects (displacement of food production to non-mapped zones) - Mining and extractive industry conflicts (particularly relevant for Sahelian shea zones) - Political economy of land tenure and conflict resolution

docs.title: 12. Multi-Actor Approach Statement
docs.text:
The call requires proposals to implement the multi-actor approach with a consortium based on a balanced mix of actors including farmers, researchers, farm accountants, and businesses.

This project fulfils this requirement through two structural mechanisms:

1. Consortium composition: The consortium includes research institutions, a cooperative federation (farmers and farm accountants), private sector supply chain analytics, technology providers, and communication specialists. Each WP Lead represents a distinct actor type.

2. Multi-Actor Panel (MAP): A formally constituted advisory and co-creation body with defined roles, meeting schedule, and budget allocation. MAP members include primary producers (shea cooperatives, olive cooperative representatives), farm accountants, EU and African policymakers, and downstream market operators. MAP activities are integrated into WP1 (co-design of framework), WP5 (co-design of policy recommendations), and WP7 (validation of communications).

Genuine co-creation, not consultation: Following Horizon Europe MAA guidance, the MAP is not a post-hoc consultation mechanism. MAP members will co-design research instruments (WP1), validate data collection approaches (WP2, WP3), co-author policy recommendations (WP5), and participate in dissemination events (WP7). Budget is allocated proportionally to ensure genuine participation.

An SSH co-lead will be designated within WP5 and will have cross-cutting advisory responsibilities across all WPs. SSH integration criteria from the Horizon Europe SSH Integration Toolkit will be applied at proposal stage and reviewed at mid-term.

docs.title: SUPPORTING CONTEXT: Why This Call Is a Strategic Fit
The EU Has Built the Regulatory Framework — Now Needs the Analytical Tools
docs.text:
In 2025–2026, the EU completed the regulatory architecture for its bioeconomy and nature market vision: - The CRCF Regulation was operationalised (November 2025) - The Nature Credits Roadmap was published (July 2025) - The EU Bioeconomy Strategy was revised - CSRD is now driving corporate Scope 3 disclosure obligations

What the EU lacks is the supply chain-resolved quantitative methodology to operationalise these frameworks. Standard LCA tools and national agricultural statistics lack the phase resolution and North-South supply chain coverage required. The True Value Framework directly fills this gap.

docs.title: The Multi-Commodity, Multi-Region Design Maximises Policy Relevance
docs.text: By spanning West Africa (GGW/shea), Mediterranean EU (olive oil/Spain/Italy), and South America (Argentina/soya), this project generates the comparative evidence base that single-commodity or single-region projects cannot produce. The EU needs to understand how bioeconomy and nature market incentives interact with food security risks across different governance environments — this project provides exactly that.

docs.title: The Cooperative Sector Is the Key Actor
docs.text: Both in the olive oil sector (Spain) and in the shea sector (West African women's cooperatives), cooperative structures are simultaneously the most vulnerable to value appropriation asymmetries AND the most capable of scaling sustainable practices if given the right analytical and policy tools. This project puts cooperatives at the centre of the research design and the multi-actor approach — not as subjects of study but as co-creators of knowledge and co-authors of policy recommendations.

docs.title: The GGW Dimension Provides Global Impact and Political Visibility
docs.text:
The Great Green Wall is the AU and EU's flagship collaborative initiative for African land restoration, climate adaptation and rural development. Connecting this project explicitly to GGW objectives — through the shea supply chain analysis and the natural capital accounting for parkland agroforestry — provides political visibility, alignment with EU–Africa partnership commitments, and a pathway to the $33 billion GGW financing challenge.

HORIZON-CL6-2026-01-CIRCBIO-09

Proposal: TRUE VALUE CHAINS — Balancing Bioeconomy, Food Security, Climate and Biodiversity Through Phase-Resolved Supply Chain Analytics

Call: HORIZON-CL6-2026-01-CIRCBIO-09Call Title: Balancing food security, bioeconomy, climate and biodiversity objectives to unlock sustainable value chainsAction Type: Research and Innovation Action (RIA)Opening Date: 17 April 2026Deadline: 17 September 2026, 17:00 Brussels timeIndicative Budget Request: €6,000,000Total Call Budget: €12,000,000Project Acronym (provisional): TrueVal-ChainsStatus: DRAFT v0.1 — April 2026Lead Author: SNJAction required from: April 2026

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

TrueVal-Chains is a 54-month, €6 million Research and Innovation Action (RIA) submitted under Horizon Europe Call HORIZON-CL6-2026-01-CIRCBIO-09: Balancing food security, bioeconomy, climate and biodiversity objectives to unlock sustainable value chains.

The Problem

The EU's bioeconomy agenda — backed by the CRCF Regulation (2025), the Nature Credits Roadmap (2025), and the revised CAP — has created a regulatory architecture that demands one thing above all else: reliable, supply-chain-resolved quantitative evidence on how agricultural value, environmental performance, and food security interact across the farm-to-market chain. That evidence does not yet exist at the resolution policymakers and markets need. Without it, carbon farming certification risks greenwashing, nature credits cannot be priced credibly, farmers remain price-takers unable to monetise their stewardship, and land-use conflict assessments remain speculative.

The Solution

This project develops, validates and deploys the True Value Framework (TVF) — a quantitative, phase-resolved supply chain intelligence methodology built to produce exactly this evidence. TVF maps each commodity supply chain into discrete, measurable phases, each defined by a physical state, a transformation, a measurable output, and a transparency classification. Across each phase, the framework accounts simultaneously for physical flows, economic value distribution, Scope 1/2/3 GHG emissions, natural capital (biodiversity, water, soil, carbon sequestration), and social equity — generating the integrated accounts that the CRCF, Nature Credits, and EU EAA frameworks require but currently lack.

Three Commodity Systems — One Comparative Framework

The project applies TVF to three strategically chosen commodity systems that together span the full range of governance environments, supply chain architectures, and policy challenges relevant to the call:

  1. Shea — West Africa to EU (anchor commodity)Mapping the full supply chain from parkland agroforestry in Senegal, Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana through to EU cosmetics and chocolate manufacturers. Shea is the most direct link between the Great Green Wall (GGW) — the AU/EU's flagship $33 billion Sahel restoration programme, currently only ~2% achieved — and EU corporate Scope 3 obligations under CSRD. The project delivers the first phase-resolved Scope 3 GHG emission factors for shea, unlocking carbon and nature credit revenue for 4–6 million women cooperative members along the GGW corridor.

  2. Olive Oil — Spain and Italy (EU cooperative anchor)Spain is the world's largest olive oil producer; cooperatives account for ~65% of production. Italy is the critical bulk trade destination — the Spain→Italy value flow is a textbook case of value appropriation asymmetry. The project delivers a cooperative business model innovation assessment, olive mill waste circular bioeconomy analysis, natural capital accounts for Andalusian olive systems, and policy recommendations benchmarked against the OECD's existing Spain policy recommendations. The ROBIN Horizon Europe project (Andalusia governance) is identified as a direct complementarity partner.

  3. Diversification Commodities — Argentine Soya/Beef and Spanish CherriesTests TVF scalability across a high-deforestation-risk Global South commodity (Argentine soya/beef, directly relevant to the EU Deforestation Regulation) and a domestically bounded EU horticultural system (Spanish cherries). Together these generate the cross-governance comparative dataset needed to make the project's policy recommendations universally applicable, not case-specific.

Methodology

TVF is grounded in the Negotiation–Definition–Contribution (N-D-C) triadic analytical structure — a formally validated framework that models each supply chain phase as a system of constraints (D), outputs (C), and emergent stable state (N). Sustainability is measured as the D/C balance: imbalance reveals structural fragility, value leakage, or environmental risk. The framework has been developed and validated on the gold supply chain (Phases 0–7) and is now extended to agricultural commodity systems. TVF is directly compatible with SEEA natural capital accounting, IPBES biodiversity valuation, the GHG Protocol Scope 3 standard, and the EU Economic Accounts for Agriculture (EAA) framework.

A minimum of 7 partners across EU Member States and Associated Countries, combining:

A formally constituted Multi-Actor Panel includes shea women's cooperatives, olive cooperative representatives, EU cosmetics and food manufacturers, farm accountants, and EU and African policymakers — fulfilling the call's genuine co-creation requirement.

1.1 The Problem This Proposal Addresses

The EU's bioeconomy and nature market strategies — including the Carbon Removals and Carbon Farming (CRCF) Regulation (EU 2025/2358), the Nature Credits Roadmap, and the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) — require a fundamental transformation of how agricultural value is measured, distributed, and governed. Yet a critical gap persists: the methods and tools for quantifying the full, phase-resolved True Value of agricultural supply chains — including their environmental, social and climate costs and benefits — are not yet operational at the farm-to-market level.

Without this analytical infrastructure, policymakers cannot credibly balance bioeconomy incentives against food security safeguards. Farmers remain price-takers, unable to demonstrate the full value of their environmental stewardship. Markets for carbon credits, nature credits, and biodiversity offsets lack the supply chain grounding needed to prevent greenwashing, perverse incentives, and land-use conflicts.

1.2 The Opportunity

This proposal develops and validates the True Value Framework (TVF) — a quantitative, phase-resolved supply chain intelligence methodology — across three strategically chosen commodity systems:

Shea (West Africa: Senegal, Burkina Faso, Mali, Ghana) — connecting the Great Green Wall (GGW) initiative and African women's cooperatives to EU cosmetics and food manufacturers

Olive Oil (Spain, with Italy as the critical bulk-trade market) — the world's largest cooperative-based agricultural commodity, anchored in proven bioeconomy governance models

Diversification commodities (Argentine soya/beef, Spanish cherries, other agri-food products) — to test framework scalability and cross-regional land-use conflict analysis

This selection is not arbitrary. These three systems together cover: (a) a North-South supply chain with deep Scope 3 GHG and biodiversity implications (Shea/GGW); (b) a mature EU cooperative sector with documented natural capital governance challenges (Olive Oil/Spain); and (c) a Global South commodity with high land-use conflict risk and AfCFTA relevance (Argentina/soya). Together they generate the comparative dataset required to produce generalizable, policy-applicable findings.

1.3 Why Now

The EU Nature Credits Roadmap (2025) requires certification methodologies that do not yet exist at supply chain resolution

The CRCF Regulation (adopted November 2025) demands monitoring, reporting and verification tools for carbon farming — tools this project will develop and test

The EU Vision for Agriculture and Food explicitly calls for "fair income for farmers" and "resilient supply chains"

The GGW received $14 billion in pledges in 2021, yet only ~2% of restoration targets have been met; this project provides the value chain intelligence to unlock that capital

The deadline (17 September 2026) aligns with growing institutional urgency to operationalize these frameworks before the 2027 CAP review cycle

  1. Research Objectives

Primary Objective

To develop, validate and deploy a phase-resolved True Value Chain (TVC) analytical framework that enables farmers, cooperatives, policymakers and market operators to quantify, balance and communicate the full spectrum of bioeconomy, food security, climate and biodiversity impacts across agricultural supply chains.

Specific Objectives

  1. Commodities and Geographic Focus

3.1 Shea — West Africa to EU (Anchor Commodity)

Why Shea:Shea is simultaneously one of the most critical bioeconomy commodities linking the Great Green Wall (GGW) to EU markets and one of the most structurally opaque supply chains in global trade. An estimated 4–6 million women in West Africa depend on shea kernel collection and processing for their primary income. EU imports of shea butter feed the cosmetics industry (notably Unilever, L'Oréal, The Body Shop supply chains) and chocolate and confectionery manufacturers (as a cocoa butter substitute) — yet Scope 3 emissions and biodiversity impacts along this chain remain unmapped at the resolution needed for credible certification.

Scope and Geography:

Senegal, Burkina Faso, Mali, Ghana (production zones along the GGW corridor)

Processing and export hubs: Bobo-Dioulasso (BF), Dakar (SN), Accra (GH)

EU import/refining: France, Germany, Netherlands, Italy

End markets: EU cosmetics and chocolate manufacturers; retail sustainability commitments

True Value Framework Application:

Phase-resolved supply chain mapping (collection → kernel processing → butter production → export → refining → manufacturing → retail)

Full Scope 3 GHG accounting per phase

Biodiversity and ecosystem services valuation (parkland agroforestry, carbon sequestration, soil health)

Women's cooperative income diversification modelling (beyond food/feed to cosmetics, energy, organic fertiliser, carbon credits)

Land-use conflict assessment: shea parkland vs agricultural intensification vs mining concessions

Connection to Great Green Wall:The GGW represents the world's largest ecosystem restoration programme (14 billion pledged by 2021). Shea agroforestry is a cornerstone of GGW land-use strategy in Senegal and Burkina Faso. This project directly addresses the documented gap: only ~2% of GGW national restoration targets achieved, partly due to absence of functioning value chain infrastructure linking restoration activities to market incentives. TVF supply chain analytics will provide the evidentiary foundation to unlock GGW-aligned carbon and nature credit mechanisms.

Key Data Partners:

National Union of Shea Producers (Burkina Faso) — 5,000 women's cooperatives

  1. Methodology — The True Value Framework (TVF)

4.1 Framework Overview

The True Value Framework (TVF) is a quantitative, phase-resolved supply chain intelligence methodology that models agricultural supply chains as structured physical and value systems, measuring at each phase:

Physical flows: mass, volume, transformation, custody transfer

Economic flows: costs, revenues, margins, value appropriation by actor type

Environmental accounts: GHG emissions (Scope 1, 2, 3), water, land, biodiversity impact

Social accounts: income distribution, labour conditions, gender equity, community impact

Governance structure: transparency, opacity classification, regulatory compliance

The methodological architecture follows the Negotiation–Definition–Contribution (N-D-C) triadic framework (Tholonic model), which structures each supply chain phase as a triadic system where:

N (Negotiation) = the stable, coherent operational state at that phase

D (Definition) = constraints, requirements and boundaries governing what the phase is

C (Contribution) = outputs, flows and connections governing what the phase does

Sustainability of any phase is measured by the D/C balance: when constraints and contributions are in equilibrium, the phase is most energy-efficient and resilient. Imbalance signals structural fragility, value leakage, or environmental risk.

This framework has been developed and validated on the gold supply chain (Phase 0–7, mineral origin to exchange-registered bullion) and is now being extended to agricultural commodity systems.

4.2 Phase Resolution

Each commodity supply chain is mapped to discrete phases, each defined by:

A physical state of the commodity

A transformation or custody change

A measurable output with units

An assigned transparency classification (High / Medium / Low / Opaque)

4.3 Natural Capital Accounting Integration

The project will develop and test natural capital accounting methods aligned with:

SEEA (System of Environmental-Economic Accounting) — the UN framework for ecosystem accounts

EU Economic Accounts for Agriculture (EAA) framework — direct call requirement

IPBES biodiversity valuation protocols

CRCF Regulation certification methodology requirements — the project will contribute input to Delegated Acts expected in 2026

For each commodity and phase, a Natural Capital Account will be constructed containing:

Provisioning ecosystem services (food, fibre, fuel)

Regulating ecosystem services (carbon sequestration, water regulation, pollination)

Cultural ecosystem services (livelihood, heritage, gender empowerment)

Biodiversity metrics (species richness, habitat quality, connectivity)

4.4 Scope 3 GHG Accounting

Full Scope 3 GHG emission accounting will be conducted for the shea supply chain as the primary pilot (with olive oil as secondary). This addresses a critical gap: cosmetics and food companies with Scope 3 disclosure obligations under CSRD (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive) lack supply chain-resolved emission factors for shea butter. The project will generate:

Per-phase GHG emission factors (kg CO₂e per kg commodity)

Attribution of emissions by supply chain actor type

Uncertainty ranges and transparency classification

Integration pathway into existing LCA databases (ecoinvent, etc.)

4.5 Biomass Threshold Modelling

A core methodological innovation is the development of biomass supply-demand threshold models — quantitative assessments of the market price levels at which bioeconomy incentives (carbon credits, nature credits, bioenergy contracts) begin to divert agricultural biomass from food/feed to non-food uses, triggering food security risks. These threshold models will be calibrated separately for each commodity system and validated against historical market data.

4.6 Land-Use Conflict Assessment

The project will apply a spatial land-use conflict index to each commodity system, assessing:

Direct competition between food production, bioeconomy crops, carbon forestry, and nature restoration

Leakage effects (displacement of food production to non-mapped zones)

Mining and extractive industry conflicts (particularly relevant for Sahelian shea zones)

Political economy of land tenure and conflict resolution

  1. Multi-Actor Approach Statement

The call requires proposals to implement the multi-actor approach with a consortium based on a balanced mix of actors including farmers, researchers, farm accountants, and businesses.

This project fulfils this requirement through two structural mechanisms:

  1. Consortium composition: The consortium includes research institutions, a cooperative federation (farmers and farm accountants), private sector supply chain analytics, technology providers, and communication specialists. Each WP Lead represents a distinct actor type.

  2. Multi-Actor Panel (MAP): A formally constituted advisory and co-creation body with defined roles, meeting schedule, and budget allocation. MAP members include primary producers (shea cooperatives, olive cooperative representatives), farm accountants, EU and African policymakers, and downstream market operators. MAP activities are integrated into WP1 (co-design of framework), WP5 (co-design of policy recommendations), and WP7 (validation of communications).

Genuine co-creation, not consultation: Following Horizon Europe MAA guidance, the MAP is not a post-hoc consultation mechanism. MAP members will co-design research instruments (WP1), validate data collection approaches (WP2, WP3), co-author policy recommendations (WP5), and participate in dissemination events (WP7). Budget is allocated proportionally to ensure genuine participation.

(To be attached: CRCF Regulation summary; Nature Credits Roadmap key elements; Delegated Acts timeline)

Annex E — Letters of Intent

(To be attached at proposal submission: letters from all consortium partners and key MAP members)

Annex F — CVs of Key Personnel

(To be attached: 2-page CVs for all key researchers and project leads)

Annex G — Ethics Self-Assessment

(To be completed: ethics checklist per EC requirements; data protection; informed consent in fieldwork; research involving vulnerable communities — shea women cooperatives)

SUPPORTING CONTEXT: Why This Call Is a Strategic Fit

The EU Has Built the Regulatory Framework — Now Needs the Analytical Tools

In 2025–2026, the EU completed the regulatory architecture for its bioeconomy and nature market vision:

The CRCF Regulation was operationalised (November 2025)

The Nature Credits Roadmap was published (July 2025)

The EU Bioeconomy Strategy was revised

CSRD is now driving corporate Scope 3 disclosure obligations

What the EU lacks is the supply chain-resolved quantitative methodology to operationalise these frameworks. Standard LCA tools and national agricultural statistics lack the phase resolution and North-South supply chain coverage required. The True Value Framework directly fills this gap.

The Multi-Commodity, Multi-Region Design Maximises Policy Relevance

By spanning West Africa (GGW/shea), Mediterranean EU (olive oil/Spain/Italy), and South America (Argentina/soya), this project generates the comparative evidence base that single-commodity or single-region projects cannot produce. The EU needs to understand how bioeconomy and nature market incentives interact with food security risks across different governance environments — this project provides exactly that.

The Cooperative Sector Is the Key Actor

Both in the olive oil sector (Spain) and in the shea sector (West African women's cooperatives), cooperative structures are simultaneously the most vulnerable to value appropriation asymmetries AND the most capable of scaling sustainable practices if given the right analytical and policy tools. This project puts cooperatives at the centre of the research design and the multi-actor approach — not as subjects of study but as co-creators of knowledge and co-authors of policy recommendations.

The GGW Dimension Provides Global Impact and Political Visibility

The Great Green Wall is the AU and EU's flagship collaborative initiative for African land restoration, climate adaptation and rural development. Connecting this project explicitly to GGW objectives — through the shea supply chain analysis and the natural capital accounting for parkland agroforestry — provides political visibility, alignment with EU–Africa partnership commitments, and a pathway to the $33 billion GGW financing challenge.

docs.title: Abstract Supply Chain Phase Template
docs.text:
Product-agnostic supply chain phase model (phases 0–8) and information categories per phase, with N-D-C tagging and example metric types. Use this template to build instances for specific commodities (e.g. shea butter, gold). The value chain (profit, pricing, margins) has a separate Abstract Value Chain Phase Template and instances (gold, shea); phases align by id only.

N-D-C: D = Definition (constraints, boundaries, specs). C = Contribution (connections, flow, integration). N = Negotiation (emergent outcome: throughput, yield, price). Each phase is the locus where D and C interact to produce N.

docs.text:

Category N-D-C Example metric type Physical state (resource in situ) D e.g. description; grade/spec if applicable Location / geography D e.g. region, country, site list; km² or ha Identification / boundary D e.g. reserve boundary; harvest area; map reference Typical time scale context e.g. years; seasonal (months); cycle Transparency level D e.g. High / Medium / Low D-parameters (constraints) D e.g. threshold; regulatory; cost limit (index or score) C-parameters (integration) C e.g. survey/tech access; partnerships; data sharing (index or score)

docs.title: Abstract Value Chain Phase Template
docs.text:
Product-agnostic value chain phase model (phases 0–8) aligned with the Abstract Supply Chain Phase Template. Each value_phase_id corresponds to the same logical stage as supply phase_id; linkage is by identifier only—no mixing of physical and value datasets.

This template defines value categories per phase (revenue, cost, margin, fees, realized price) with N-D-C tagging and example value metric types. Instances: Gold value instance, Shea value instance.

N-D-C (value interpretation): D = Definition (cost constraints, contract terms, regulatory/tax). C = Contribution (counterparty options, flexibility, market access). N = Negotiation (revenue, margin, realized price, value capture). Time resolution: quarterly and/or annual (period end date).

docs.title: N-D-C Definitions Reference Guide
docs.text:
How the D (Definition) and C (Contribution) values are defined, where they come from, and how to research them further.

This document is written for someone who wants to understand the intellectual and data sources behind the N-D-C model in this project, audit the current values, or extend the model with real empirical data.

docs.title: The Short Version
docs.text: What Where What D and C mean conceptually for each phase docs/Research/NDC_QUALITATIVE_D_AND_C_MAPPING_BY_PHASE.md The named D and C parameters per phase (structured) schema/supply_chain_phases_ndc.csv The D-natural vs D-institutional distinction docs/Research/NDC_QUALITATIVE_D_AND_C_MAPPING_BY_PHASE.md (Part 1) The math (how D, C → N, balance score) docs/PDI/NDC_D_C_N_METRICS_CALCULATION_REFERENCE.md Where the current numeric D/C values come from schema/gold_supply_chain_metrics_ndc.csv (synthetic) Real-world evidence grounding Phases 1–2 src/frontend/project/gold/data/processed/phase1_summary.json, phase2_summary.json The tholonic framework behind the model docs/Research/../Research/THOLONIC_FRAMEWORK_SUPPLY_AND_VALUE_CHAIN_APPLICATION.md The template for any new phase instance docs/PDI/ABSTRACT_SUPPLY_CHAIN_PHASE_TEMPLATE.md The gold supply chain as a filled-in instance docs/PDI/ABSTRACT_SUPPLY_CHAIN_PHASE_TEMPLATE_GOLD_INSTANCE.md

docs.title: What is D?
docs.text:
D (Definition) represents all constraints, boundaries, specifications, and requirements that define what a supply chain phase is. D parameters are internally focused — they govern structure, identity, and what is permissible or possible within the phase.

D is not a single number in the real world. It is the sum of multiple constraint parameters, each scored 0–100:

D_total = D1 + D2 + D3 + D4 + ... + Dn

Typical total range: 150–350 (dimensionless index)

docs.title: What is C?
docs.text:
C (Contribution) represents all connections, outputs, integrations, and flows that define what a supply chain phase does — how it connects to the world outside itself. C parameters are externally focused — they govern production, relationships, and what the phase delivers forward.

C_total = C1 + C2 + C3 + C4 + ... + Cn

Typical total range: 150–350 (dimensionless index)

docs.title: What is N?
docs.text:
N (Negotiation) is not directly measured — it emerges from the interaction of D and C. It represents the operational coherence of the phase: its actual throughput, stability, and sustainable capacity.

balance_score = 100 × e^(−2 × |D − C| / max(D, C))

N = √(D × C) × (balance_score / 100)

N is highest when D ≈ C (balanced). When D far exceeds C, or C far exceeds D, the balance score collapses and N follows.

Full derivation: docs/PDI/NDC_D_C_N_METRICS_CALCULATION_REFERENCE.md

docs.title: Part 2 — The D-Natural vs D-Institutional Distinction
docs.text:
This is the most important conceptual refinement in the project. Not all constraints are the same kind of thing.

Class Origin Can be changed? Example D-natural Physics, chemistry, geology, biology No — governed by natural law Minimum ore grade for economic extraction D-institutional States, law, financial institutions, industry bodies Yes — contingent on politics and negotiation LBMA purity standard (99.99%), royalty rates, export licences

D-natural parameters would exist in a world with no governments, no laws, and no institutions. They arise from the physical nature of what is being done.

D-institutional parameters are the encoded outcomes of negotiations between states, corporations, and market bodies. They are imported into the supply chain phase from the political and legal context that surrounds it. They feel natural — they are treated as fixed constraints — but they were constructed and can, in principle, be changed.

This distinction matters for two reasons:

  1. Transparency and opacity: Opacity arising from D-natural is genuinely irreducible. No reform can make an ore body more visible. Opacity from D-institutional is contingent — it was constructed and can be reformed.

  2. Value capture: D-institutional parameters are the primary levers through which value is redirected away from producers. Royalty rates, accreditation requirements, and purity standards all determine who may participate in the chain and on what terms.

In the parameter tables below, each D parameter is tagged [natural] or [institutional] where known.

Primary source: docs/Research/NDC_QUALITATIVE_D_AND_C_MAPPING_BY_PHASE.md, section "The Two Classes of D"

docs.title: Part 3 — The Named Parameters for Each Phase
docs.text: These are the canonical D and C parameters defined in schema/supply_chain_phases_ndc.csv. Each parameter is a named index variable (0–100 scale) that represents the intensity or degree of that constraint or integration at the phase level.

docs.title: Phase 0 — Geological Occurrence & Prospecting
docs.text:
Parameter Role Type Description D1: ore_grade_threshold D natural Minimum grade below which deposit is uneconomic D2: geological_certainty D natural Confidence level in resource classification (measured/indicated/inferred) D3: exploration_cost_limit D institutional Capital budget ceiling for exploration activities D4: regulatory_constraints D institutional Permitting, environmental assessment, indigenous rights requirements C1: survey_technology C — Availability and quality of seismic, drilling, remote sensing capability C2: data_sharing C — Access to public geological databases, historical surveys C3: exploration_partnerships C — Joint venture partners, co-investment agreements C4: market_information C — Gold price signals, demand outlook — informs exploration priority

Balance target: 0.75 | Transparency: Medium

docs.title: Phase 1 — Mine Extraction
docs.text:
Parameter Role Type Description D1: ore_grade_actual D natural Actual grade of ore being extracted (g/t) — set by geology D2: extraction_method_spec D natural Physical constraints of open-pit vs underground vs heap leach D3: safety_standards D institutional National and international safety regulations D4: environmental_regulations D institutional Tailings, air quality, water discharge standards D5: production_capacity D mixed Physical throughput ceiling (natural); royalty/tax obligations (institutional) C1: equipment_suppliers C — Availability and diversity of mining equipment supply chain C2: labor_flexibility C — Workforce availability, skills, union constraints C3: energy_sources C — Access to grid electricity, diesel, renewable — type and reliability C4: transportation_options C — Road, rail, air options for ore and personnel C5: market_access C — Offtake agreements, refinery relationships, export routes

Balance target: 0.85 | Transparency: High

Real-world evidence in project data (src/frontend/project/gold/data/processed/phase1_summary.json): - D-institutional confirmed: LBMA Responsible Gold Guidance — verified by Newmont customer audits at Ahafo South, Lihir, Yanacocha - D-natural evidence: 192 ha land reclamation (2024) — confirms irreducible physical closure obligations - C-fragility flag: 24% of supplier base carries elevated human rights risk (194/812 screened) - Economic scale: Newmont contributed USD 16.0B direct economic value and USD 69M community investment (2024)

docs.title: Phase 2 — Ore Processing & Concentration
docs.text:
Parameter Role Type Description D1: recovery_rate_target D natural Chemistry-constrained maximum extraction efficiency D2: process_specifications D natural Leaching, flotation, CIL protocol requirements D3: purity_standards D institutional Downstream buyer specifications for concentrate grade D4: throughput_capacity D natural Physical mill and leach pad capacity ceiling D5: waste_management D institutional Tailings dam regulations, cyanide handling standards C1: chemical_suppliers C — Cyanide, lime, flocculant supply chain C2: technology_integration C — Process control systems, automation level C3: water_sources C — Water availability — most intensive water phase in the chain C4: byproduct_markets C — Silver, copper, and other metals recovered alongside gold C5: information_systems C — Assay data, production reporting, metallurgical accounting

Balance target: 0.90 | Transparency: High

Real-world evidence in project data (src/frontend/project/gold/data/processed/phase2_summary.json): - C-parameter water: 71% water recycling rate (Newmont 2024) vs 65% baseline (2018) — positive C trend - D-natural cyanide: 30 cyanide spills in 2024 (-33% YoY) — irreducible D-natural constraint, cannot be eliminated, only reduced - Data gap: throughput volumes, recovery rates, treatment costs remain MISSING in current schema

docs.title: Phase 3 — Doré Production
docs.text:
Parameter Role Type Description D1: dore_purity_range D mixed Physical chemistry of smelting (natural); buyer purity spec (institutional) D2: smelting_protocols D natural Furnace temperature, flux requirements, pour specifications D3: bar_weight_specs D institutional Weight tolerances set by refinery acceptance standards D4: quality_control D institutional Assay and sampling protocols required by downstream C1: refinery_network C — Number and proximity of accredited refineries C2: transport_providers C — Secure transport options for doré shipment C3: assay_services C — Independent assay houses for dispute resolution C4: trade_relationships C — Refinery offtake agreements, hedging relationships

Balance target: 0.70 | Transparency: Medium

docs.title: Phase 4 — Refining
docs.text:
Parameter Role Type Description D1: fineness_standard D institutional 99.99% (four nines) purity — LBMA Good Delivery standard D2: accreditation_requirements D institutional LBMA, COMEX, and national bank approval — barrier to entry D3: refining_capacity D natural Physical throughput ceiling of electrolytic/Miller/Wohlwill plant D4: process_control D natural Chemical precision requirements of acid and electrolytic processes D5: waste_recovery D institutional Environmental compliance for acid, chlorine, and slag waste C1: client_base C — Mine operators, central banks, bullion dealers as customers C2: equipment_vendors C — Specialist refinery equipment supply chain C3: certification_bodies C — LBMA, national assay offices C4: market_integration C — Spot market access, bullion bank relationships C5: technology_adoption C — Continuous casting, inline assay, digital traceability

Balance target: 0.75 | Transparency: Medium

Note: Phase 4 carries the heaviest D-institutional burden in the chain. The LBMA Good Delivery List is a private accreditation system maintained by a London-based industry association. Access to global bullion markets depends on appearing on this list — a requirement that did not arise from the physics of refining.

docs.title: Phase 5 — Bar Casting & Assay
docs.text:
Parameter Role Type Description D1: bar_specifications D institutional LBMA Good Delivery bar: 350–430 troy oz, 99.5% minimum fineness D2: assay_precision D natural Measurement precision limits of fire assay and XRF D3: serial_protocols D institutional Hallmarking, serial numbering, tamper-evidence requirements D4: storage_standards D institutional Vault acceptance standards for bar condition D5: quality_rejection_limits D institutional Defect tolerances before bar is rejected from Good Delivery C1: exchange_relationships C — COMEX, LBMA, and other exchange approval pathways C2: vault_network C — Approved vaults accepting newly cast bars C3: transport_logistics C — Secure logistics providers certified for bullion C4: documentation_systems C — Chain of custody documentation, digital provenance records

Balance target: 0.80 | Transparency: Medium-High

docs.title: Phase 6 — Logistics & Vaulting
docs.text:
Parameter Role Type Description D1: vault_capacity D natural Physical storage capacity ceiling D2: security_protocols D institutional Insurance and regulatory minimum security specifications D3: insurance_requirements D institutional Lloyd's of London and specialist bullion insurer requirements D4: custody_standards D institutional Legal custody transfer requirements; allocated vs unallocated D5: jurisdictional_compliance D institutional AML, KYC, sanctions compliance in each vault jurisdiction C1: vault_network_size C — Number of interconnected vaults globally C2: transport_flexibility C — Air, road, sea options and frequency C3: insurance_access C — Availability of specialist bullion insurance C4: client_access C — Counterparty relationships permitting gold withdrawal C5: information_opacity C — (Note: this is a negative C parameter — opacity reduces integration)

Balance target: 0.50 | Transparency: Low (structural bottleneck)

Note: Phase 6 is the known bottleneck in the current model (D=204, C=161, balance≈65). The D-institutional burden (insurance, custody law, jurisdictional compliance) significantly exceeds the C integration capacity. This is not a data artifact — it reflects the structural reality that vault custody is controlled by a small number of approved operators, entry is restricted, and information about holdings is commercially and legally protected.

docs.title: Phase 7 — Exchange Registration
docs.text:
Parameter Role Type Description D1: exchange_standards D institutional COMEX and LBMA delivery specifications D2: registration_requirements D institutional Warrant issuance, bar inspection, weighing protocols D3: warehouse_specifications D institutional Approved warehouse location and security standards D4: delivery_protocols D institutional Last trading day, delivery notice procedures D5: contract_terms D institutional Contract size (100 oz), grade, fineness, brand requirements C1: market_participants C — Number and diversity of registered trading participants C2: clearing_systems C — CME Clearing, LCH Clearnet integration C3: information_transparency C — Daily inventory reporting — highest transparency in the chain C4: settlement_flexibility C — EFP, EFS, and block trade mechanisms C5: global_integration C — Cross-listing, arbitrage mechanisms connecting COMEX/LBMA/SGE

Balance target: 0.85 | Transparency: High

docs.title: Phase 8 — Recycling & Recovery
docs.text:
Parameter Role Type Description D1: collection_standards D institutional AML requirements for scrap gold dealers D2: sorting_protocols D natural Minimum purity levels viable for secondary smelting D3: refining_specifications D natural Chemistry of secondary refining (same as Phase 4) D4: purity_requirements D institutional Final product must meet same LBMA standard as virgin gold D5: throughput_capacity D natural Physical capacity of secondary refining infrastructure C1: waste_supplier_network C — Jewellery scrap, electronics, industrial gold waste collectors C2: refinery_relationships C — Access to Phase 4 refineries willing to accept secondary feed C3: technology_providers C — Urban mining technology, electrochemical recovery C4: market_integration C — Certified recycled gold premium, ESG buyer demand C5: regulatory_compliance C — Responsible recycling certification (RJC, LBMA)

Balance target: 0.80 | Transparency: Low-Medium

Note: Phase 8 feeds back into Phase 4 (Refining), creating the only circular loop in the supply chain. It currently supplies approximately 28% of annual gold demand. The D-institutional burden is significantly lower than Phase 4 for the same chemistry because secondary feed does not require LBMA accreditation to enter the refining step — but the output must still meet LBMA Good Delivery standard.

docs.title: Part 4 — Where the Numeric D/C Values Come From
Current Status: Synthetic Baseline
docs.text:
The numeric D and C values currently used in the simulator (e.g., Phase 1: D=270, C=277) are synthetically generated, not measured from real-world data.

Source file: schema/gold_supply_chain_metrics_ndc.csv

Every record in this file carries: 

source_type = "simulated"
source_name = "Synthetic Generator - Baseline"
notes = "Baseline balanced scenario - healthy supply chain"

How they were generated: src/data/synthetic_data_generator.py

The generator uses phase-specific D and C base values with added Gaussian noise to simulate daily variation over a 365-day period. The base values were chosen to produce balance scores consistent with each phase's expected transparency level and operational stability:

Phase D base C base Design intent 0 — Prospecting 220 210 Moderately balanced, medium transparency 1 — Mining 260 250 Near-balanced, high transparency 2 — Ore Processing 280 275 Near-balanced, high transparency, high energy 3 — Doré Production 240 235 Slightly D-dominant, medium transparency 4 — Refining 270 260 Slightly D-dominant, institutional burden 5 — Bar Casting 260 255 Near-balanced, standard protocol 6 — Logistics/Vaulting 200 195 Intentionally bottlenecked in some scenarios 7 — Exchange 280 275 Near-balanced, high transparency

The "day 1" values from this generator (the baseline scenario, record_ids 1–8 in the CSV) become the canonical simulator baseline values stored in data/frontend/gold_supply_chain_ui.json.

docs.title: What remains MISSING (and must be treated as OPAQUE)
docs.text:
Per the project's transparency classification rules, the following are explicitly absent from current data for Phase 2 and most other phases: - Throughput volumes (t ore/year, oz Au/year) - Recovery rates (%) - Treatment costs - Reagent consumption - Custody transfer records

These are the primary N-state metrics for most phases. Until they are populated, the numeric D/C values remain synthetic estimates.

docs.title: Part 6 — How to Research and Replace the Synthetic Values
Step 1: Identify the parameter you want to ground
docs.text: Use schema/supply_chain_phases_ndc.csv to find the specific parameter name (e.g., D1:ore_grade_actual for Phase 1).

docs.title: Step 2: Find a real-world source
docs.text:
Recommended public sources by phase:

Phase Best public sources 0 — Prospecting S&P Global Market Intelligence, National geological surveys (USGS, Geoscience Australia) 1 — Mining Newmont, Barrick, AngloGold annual/sustainability reports; World Gold Council production statistics 2 — Ore Processing Same major company reports; ICMM (International Council on Mining and Metals) 3 — Doré Production Largely opaque; doré assay reports are commercially confidential 4 — Refining LBMA Good Delivery list (public); individual refinery sustainability reports (Rand, Argor-Heraeus, etc.) 5 — Bar Casting LBMA Good Delivery rules (public document); COMEX delivery specifications 6 — Logistics LBMA vault list (partially public); Insurance market data (Lloyd's) — largely opaque 7 — Exchange COMEX daily inventory reports (public, free); LBMA clearing statistics (public) 8 — Recycling World Gold Council Gold Demand Trends (quarterly, free); IPMI (precious metals recyclers)

For Scope 1/2 emissions specifically: - World Gold Council "Gold and Climate" report (annual, free) - Foran et al. 2005 Balancing Act Volumes 1 and 2 (available in docs/) - Company Scope 1/2 disclosures in sustainability reports (CDP database, free) - ICCT transport emissions benchmarks (for Phase 6)

docs.title: Step 3: Score the parameter (0–100 scale)
docs.text:
Each D and C parameter is scored as an intensity index: - 0 = no constraint / no connection - 50 = moderate, typical industry level - 100 = maximum constraint / fully integrated

A regulatory burden of 100 means the highest level of regulatory friction observed anywhere in the global industry. A supplier network of 100 means maximum diversity and resilience. These are relative, comparative scores — not physical measurements.

docs.title: Step 4: Update the data store
docs.text:
Add the real value to schema/gold_supply_chain_metrics.csv with: - phase_id = the phase number - entity = the company or sector name - metric_name = the parameter ID (e.g., D1_ore_grade_actual) - metric_value = your score (0–100) - source_type = public / paid / private / inferred - source_name = citation

Then run python3 src/api/generate_ui_data.py --gold-only to propagate the update into the JSON and simulator.
