docs.title: The Tholonic Model and the True Value Pricing Convergence Index
The Problem with Commodity Prices
docs.text:
When gold trades at a given price on a commodity exchange, that price reflects everything the market knows at that moment: supply and demand signals, futures positions, macroeconomic expectations, and speculative flows. What it does not reflect is the structural reality of the chain that produced the gold. The exchange has no visibility into whether the mine that extracted the ore was operating sustainably. It cannot see whether the refinery was appropriately compensated. It has no way to measure whether the value amplification that occurred across eight distinct phases of processing was distributed in proportion to the physical and institutional work each phase contributed. The price is informationally efficient in a narrow sense, but it is structurally blind.

This gap between market price and structural reality is not unique to gold. It appears in any commodity chain that is long, opaque, and governed by terminal-market price discovery. The mines, processors, and logistics operators upstream of the exchange are price-takers in a system that sets prices without seeing them.

The Tholonic model addresses this gap by providing a formal, mathematically grounded framework for measuring structural coherence in supply and value chains. The True Value Pricing Convergence Index (TVPCI) is the diagnostic instrument that framework produces: a score that measures how closely a market price reflects what the chain's own structure can actually sustain.

docs.title: The Tholonic Framework
docs.text:
The Tholonic model is built on a simple observation: any stable, self-sustaining system can be described in terms of three structural roles.

The first role is Definition (D): the constraints, boundaries, and internal requirements that determine what a thing is. For a mine, D includes ore grade thresholds, extraction specifications, regulatory permits, and the geological reality of the deposit. These define what the mine is and what it can do.

The second role is Contribution (C): the outputs, flows, and external relationships that determine what a thing does. For a mine, C includes the ore volume it produces, the custody transfer it executes, the value it passes forward into the next phase of the chain. C is the mine's engagement with everything beyond itself.

The third role is Negotiation (N): the stable, operational entity that emerges when D and C are in sufficient balance. The N-state is not a fixed target that someone designs in advance. It is the entity that exists when the internal constraints and external contributions are proportionate. A productive, operating mine is the N-state of its phase. When D and C fall badly out of balance, the N-state degrades: the mine operates below capacity, defers investment, or closes.

The relationship between D, C, and N is recursive. The N-state of one phase becomes the starting condition for the next. Each phase in a supply chain is a self-contained D-C-N system, and the chain as a whole is a larger D-C-N system composed of its phases.

The central principle of the Tholonic model is this: systems are most stable and efficient when D and C are in approximate balance. Imbalance in either direction increases the structural cost of sustaining the system. An over-constrained phase (D dominates) produces less than its inputs demand. An under-constrained phase (C dominates) produces more than it can sustainably support. Both conditions propagate stress to adjacent phases and ultimately compromise the coherence of the chain as a whole.

This is not a metaphor. It is a measurable structural condition with quantifiable consequences.

docs.title: From Structure to Mathematics
docs.text:
The Tholonic framework was not derived from economic theory. It was derived from the simplest possible formal foundation: binary counting from zero and one.

Starting from zero and one, binary expansion produces the minimum stable forms in each dimension. Four binary states map to four points, and four non-coplanar points define a tetrahedron, the minimum stable three-dimensional structure. The recursive application of this structure produces three axis values that govern how its roles relate to one another. Those axis values turn out to be the first three prime numbers: 2, 3, and 5. They are not assigned by choice. They emerge from the geometry of the recursion itself.

When those three primes are used to seed a recursive formula, five fundamental mathematical constants emerge as natural attractors:

Constant Role in the model Value φ (phi) Coherence: the proportion of healthy, self-similar growth 1.618 e Decay: the rate at which imbalance propagates through a system 2.718 ln(2) Doubling: the natural unit of proportional value amplification 0.693 √2 Threshold: the structural crossing point between scale regimes 1.414 π/4 Equilibrium: whether the value cycle closes and returns to its origin 0.785

These constants are not borrowed from mathematics and fitted to the model. Each one is the attractor of a specific recursive architecture seeded from the same four values: 1, 2, 3, and 5. The model was built from irreducible foundations, and the constants it produces are themselves irreducible. This matters for supply chain analysis because it means the benchmarks against which each phase is measured are not set by any organization or market convention. They are structural properties of self-sustaining systems in general.

docs.title: Five Dimensions, Five Questions
docs.text:
Each of the five constants describes a different structural aspect of a supply chain, and each corresponds to a question that a different class of stakeholder needs answered.

φ (Coherence): Is this chain operating at its structural capacity? In a coherent chain, the value amplification from one phase to the next tends toward φ ≈ 1.618. Phases that amplify far above this ratio are extracting disproportionate value relative to their structural contribution. Phases that amplify far below it are under-rewarded and structurally at risk of degradation. φ is the only constant in the model that does not respond to any single lever: it improves only when all other structural dimensions are in better balance simultaneously. It is not a stakeholder question. It is a structural verdict on the chain as a whole.

e (Decay): Is this chain safe to depend on? When D and C fall out of balance at any phase, the imbalance does not stay local. It propagates to adjacent phases at a rate governed by e. This is the question asked by anyone who needs the chain to remain functional regardless of disruption: central banks holding the commodity as a reserve, governments dependent on royalty revenues, communities whose livelihoods depend on continuous operation. The e dimension identifies where the chain is most vulnerable to cascading failure, and therefore where stabilizing intervention produces the greatest systemic return.

ln(2) (Doubling): Does value reach those who created it? The total amplification of value from raw resource to finished product can be measured in natural doubling steps. The ln(2) dimension asks which phases capture which steps. A chain where terminal-market phases capture seven of eight doubling steps while primary producers capture less than one is structurally imbalanced in a quantifiable way, independent of whether anyone considers that outcome fair or unfair. It is a structural measurement, not a moral judgment, and it points to a specific structural instability: primary producers operating without adequate return will eventually stop producing.

√2 (Threshold): Is this an investment opportunity? The √2 threshold marks the boundary between two types of constraint that govern supply chain phases. The upstream phases of most physical commodity chains are dominated by inherited constraints: geology, physics, chemistry, and biology. These set hard limits that institutional decisions cannot override. The downstream phases are increasingly dominated by imposed constraints: accreditation standards, exchange delivery rules, custody law, and certification regimes. These are real and binding, but they are institutional constructions that can in principle be reformed. Investment that shifts a phase from the inherited-constraint regime into the imposed-constraint regime, by improving logistics access, opening certification pathways, or reducing unnecessary regulatory burden, produces a structurally discontinuous gain. √2 marks where that crossing occurs.

π/4 (Equilibrium): Is this chain ecologically balanced? π/4 measures whether the value and material cycles close. A chain that extracts without restoring, or where terminal-market value does not return to sustain upstream production, is consuming its own foundation. In the gold chain, recycling represents approximately 28% of total supply, and when gold prices rose 67% in one year, recycling volume grew only 3%. In a structurally coherent cycle, a terminal price signal of that magnitude would propagate back through the chain and stimulate its closure mechanism proportionally. The muted response indicates that the material cycle and the value cycle are structurally disconnected. π/4 measures exactly this gap.

docs.title: The True Value Pricing Convergence Index
docs.text:
The TVPCI combines the five dimensions into a single convergence score that answers one question: how closely does the current market price reflect the structural coherence of the chain that produced the commodity?

A TVPCI score approaching 1 indicates strong convergence. The market price and the structural state of the chain are aligned. A score below 1 indicates that the market price exceeds what the chain's structural coherence can sustain. The chain is being priced as though it were more coherent than it actually is. A score above 1 indicates that the market price falls short of what the chain's structural coherence implies. The chain is more structurally sound than the price reflects, typically because upstream producers are capturing too little of the value they create.

In practice, most long commodity chains with opaque upstream phases and terminal-market price-setting will produce TVPCI scores below 1 at the aggregate level, because market price tends to over-represent imposed-constraint phases and under-represent inherited-constraint phases. The most valuable use of the TVPCI is at the phase level, where above-1 readings identify phases whose structural performance is being systematically under-compensated.

The TVPCI is not a replacement for market price analysis. It is a second instrument that answers a different question. Market price asks what a buyer will pay today. The TVPCI asks what the chain can actually sustain over time, and whether the current price reflects that reality.

The framework also functions as an optimization instrument. It does not merely identify where structural gaps exist. It identifies which interventions, specifically those that reduce D-C imbalance at the most critical phases, would produce the greatest improvement in overall chain coherence. A phase where D is heavily loaded by legitimate constraints but C is suppressed by unnecessary institutional barriers is one where targeted reform raises the TVPCI score without touching the inherited physical constraints that define the phase.

docs.title: Practical Applications
docs.text:
For primary producers: The TVPCI provides a formal, quantitative basis for arguing that upstream phases are structurally under-rewarded. The ln(2) and φ dimensions measure this directly. When those scores show that inherited-constraint phases capture a small fraction of total chain amplification, the argument is no longer a narrative claim about fairness. It is a structural measurement grounded in the same mathematics that governs all self-sustaining systems.

For investors: The e decay dimension identifies where structural imbalance is most likely to cascade into financial damage. A chain with high decay contributions at critical phases will translate structural problems into financial problems faster than one with lower decay rates. The TVPCI flags structural stress conditions before they are visible in supply or price data.

For policymakers: The inherited/imposed distinction clarifies which imbalances are addressable by institutional reform and which are not. A regulation that targets an inherited constraint as though it were institutional in origin will be ineffective. The TVPCI provides the structural map that policy intervention requires.

For any structured physical chain: The Tholonic framework imposes no commodity-specific assumptions. The five constants are structural properties of any recursive system with D and C components. The TVPCI methodology applies wherever phase-level data can be assembled: copper, shea butter, lithium, cobalt, agricultural value chains, and beyond. Each additional case study both tests the framework's generality and adds to a comparative database of structural coherence scores across commodity types and chain architectures.

The full technical derivation of the Tholonic model, including the mathematical proof that the five constants emerge necessarily from the same recursive architecture seeded by the first three prime numbers, is presented in TVPCI_FOUNDATION.md.

End of introduction

docs.title: The TrueValue Pricing Convergence Index
docs.text: A plain-language explanation

docs.title: The Problem: Prices Carry No Structural Information
docs.text:
When a kilogram of shea butter concentrate leaves a collector in Burkina Faso for \$0.15 and arrives on a European shelf as body butter worth \$47.50, something significant happened in between. Six or seven supply chain steps added processing, logistics, packaging, branding, and retail margin. The price at each end is real. But the price at the retail end tells you nothing about how those intermediate steps were structured, who captured value at each one, whether the chain is environmentally sustainable, or whether the woman who spent a day harvesting shea nuts is being compensated in proportion to her contribution.

A market price is informationally efficient in the narrow sense: it reflects all available market signals at the point of sale. But it is structurally blind. It does not contain the structural state of the chain that produced the good.

The True Value Pricing Convergence Index (TVPCI) measures the gap between a market price and the price that the structural state of the chain would support. It does not say what the correct price should be. It says how well the current price reflects what the chain actually is.

The score runs from 0 to 100. A score of 100 means the market price and the structural value of the chain are fully aligned. A score near 0 means the price and the chain structure are effectively disconnected. Most real supply chains score somewhere between 35 and 75, with the exact position depending on how balanced, proportional, and transparent the individual phases are.

docs.title: The Framework: N, D, and C
docs.text:
The TVPCI is built on a structural model of how any functioning system works. Every operational entity, whether a mine, a refinery, a logistics provider, or a farming cooperative, has three structural properties:

N (the operational state): The stable, functioning entity itself. For a mine, N is the producing mine. For a refinery, N is the operating refinery. N is not something you can measure directly. It emerges from the balance between D and C.

D (Definition and Constraint): Everything that defines what the entity must do and what it must comply with. Physical requirements, regulatory standards, technical specifications, minimum viable inputs. D is internally focused. It governs structure and identity.

C (Contribution and Connection): Everything the entity produces and passes forward. Material outputs, custody transfers, market connections, the options available to it. C is externally focused. It governs flow and relationship.

A phase is structurally coherent when D and C are roughly in balance: what the phase requires to operate is proportionate to what it produces. When D far exceeds C (the phase is heavily constrained but poorly connected), the operational entity struggles to sustain itself. When C far exceeds D (the phase contributes more than its constraints can support), it is drawing down reserves or cutting structural corners.

This model is not an abstract philosophy. The values N, D, and C are measurable. D is quantified by counting and weighting the constraints a phase operates under. C is quantified by counting and weighting the outputs and options the phase has available. N is the operational capacity that emerges from that balance.

docs.title: Why Mathematics Is Involved
docs.text:
The N-D-C model is not simply descriptive. When the framework's own recursive rules are applied mathematically (using the structural values of the model as starting seeds), five fundamental mathematical constants emerge as natural attractors:

Constant Value Role in the TVPCI $\varphi$ 1.618 Coherence: the natural amplification ratio between healthy phases $e$ 2.718 Decay: how quickly imbalance propagates across phases $\ln(2)$ 0.693 Doubling: the unit of value amplification through the chain $\sqrt{2}$ 1.414 Threshold: the structural crossing point between constraint regimes $\pi/4$ 0.785 Equilibrium: whether the value cycle closes and returns to its origin

These constants are not chosen because they are mathematically famous. They emerge from the structure of the model itself, in the same way that $\varphi$ emerges from the Fibonacci sequence without being put there. The derivation is given in full in the TVPCI Foundation document. For the purposes of this explanation, what matters is what they measure.

docs.title: The Five Dimensions
docs.text: Each constant answers a different structural question about a supply chain phase.

docs.title: $\varphi$: Is each phase amplifying value in natural proportion?
docs.text:
In a structurally coherent chain, the operational capacity of each phase should be approximately 1.618 times the capacity of the prior phase. This is not an arbitrary target. It is the ratio that emerges when a self-similar system grows by passing a proportion of its current state forward to the next level. The same ratio appears in the Fibonacci sequence, the growth of shells, and the branching of trees, because all of those systems follow the same proportional inheritance rule.

When the ratio between consecutive phases is close to $\varphi$, value is passing through the chain naturally. When the ratio falls far below $\varphi$, value is being extracted or suppressed at that boundary. When it far exceeds $\varphi$, an unstable amplification is occurring.

Gold chain example: From the bar casting phase (Phase 5) to the vaulting and logistics phase (Phase 6), operational capacity drops from a normalised score of 237 to 118. The ratio is 0.498. The structural target is 1.618. This is the most severe boundary distortion in the entire gold chain, and it points directly at the vaulting phase as the structural bottleneck.

Shea chain example: The full chain amplifies farmgate value by a factor of 317. In a structurally coherent chain, that amplification would be distributed across the phases in $\varphi$-proportional steps. Instead, nearly all of it concentrates at the European manufacturing and retail end, and almost none returns to the collector. The $\varphi$ score for the shea chain is very low.

docs.title: $e$: How quickly does imbalance spread?
docs.text:
When D and C diverge significantly within a phase, the N-state of that phase begins to degrade. Critically, the degradation does not stay local. It propagates to adjacent phases at a rate governed by $e$. This is because $e$ is the unique constant where a system's rate of change equals its current state: imbalance grows at the same rate as the imbalance itself.

The $e$ dimension of the TVPCI identifies which phases are most vulnerable to cascading failure. A chain with a high $e$-decay contribution at a critical phase is fragile: a mine closure, a regulatory intervention, or a logistics disruption at that phase will cascade rapidly rather than being absorbed locally.

docs.title: $\ln(2)$: Who captures each step of value growth?
docs.text:
Every supply chain amplifies the value of raw inputs as they move toward the terminal market. Each doubling of value is one $\ln(2)$ step. A chain that multiplies farmgate value by 300 contains approximately 8.2 natural doubling steps ($\ln(300) / \ln(2) \approx 8.2$).

The $\ln(2)$ dimension does not ask how many doublings occur in total. It asks which phases capture which steps. A chain where terminal-market phases capture 7 of 8 doubling steps while primary producers capture less than 1 is structurally imbalanced in a quantifiable way, regardless of whether the terminal market price is "correct" by conventional measures.

docs.title: $\sqrt{2}$: Has the chain crossed its structural threshold?
docs.text:
$\sqrt{2}$ marks the geometric mean of 1 and 2, the smallest incommensurable scale change, and the structural crossing point between two distinct regimes. Below the $\sqrt{2}$ threshold, a phase is operating in a regime where physical and geological constraints set the ceiling. Above it, the chain has crossed into a regime where institutional and commercial structures set the terms.

Investment that moves a phase across this threshold produces a structurally discontinuous improvement, not merely a marginal one. The $\sqrt{2}$ dimension identifies where those crossing points are.

docs.title: $\pi/4$: Does the value cycle close?
docs.text:
A supply chain is not only a forward flow. The value that reaches the terminal market must, in a structurally healthy chain, complete a circuit: investment flows back to the phases that produced the value, sustaining future production, renewing ecological resources, and compensating the people whose labour created the chain. $\pi/4$ measures whether this circuit closes.

A chain where terminal-market value does not return to primary producers has a broken cycle. The gold chain's Phase 8 (recycling and recovery) is the physical expression of this closure mechanism: gold already in the market re-enters the refining process, reducing the burden on primary extraction. Measuring whether that cycle is structurally complete is the $\pi/4$ question.

docs.title: The Five Stakeholder Questions
docs.text:
The five dimensions are not only technical measurements. Each one corresponds to a distinct question that a different class of stakeholder needs answered:

Constant The question Who asks it $\pi/4$ Is this chain ecologically balanced? Environmental advocates, affected communities, future generations $\sqrt{2}$ Is this an investment opportunity? Capital, development finance, institutional investors $e$ Is this chain safe to depend on? Central banks, regulators, governments, long-duration holders $\ln(2)$ Does value reach those who created it? Primary producers, communities, resource agencies $\varphi$ Is the chain operating at its structural capacity? No single stakeholder: emerges only when all four dimensions are in balance simultaneously

The $\varphi$ question is categorically different from the other four. Its formula does not depend on D or C directly. It measures the attractor state for a fully resolved system, the value the chain approaches when all structural tensions have been addressed. No single stakeholder can produce that outcome by acting alone. $\varphi$ is the verdict that arrives only after the other four questions have been answered.

docs.title: Building the Score: Three Components
docs.text: The TVPCI combines the five dimensions into three operational checks, then applies a correction for missing information.

docs.title: Check 1: Phase balance (40% of the score)
docs.text:
For each phase $i$, the balance score is:

$$B_i = 1 - \frac{|D_i - C_i|}{D_i + C_i}$$

A score of 1 indicates perfect balance between constraints and connections. A score near 0 indicates that one side completely dominates. The balance score for the chain is the average across all phases, weighted by phase importance.

The base of the balance formula uses $e$ as the decay constant. When D and C diverge, the effective balance score decays at the $e$-governed rate, reflecting the fact that imbalance is self-amplifying.

Why it matters: A phase where constraints far exceed connections forces every participant to spend structural energy simply surviving within the system rather than contributing to it. The gold vaulting phase has D = 420 (security law, insurance minimums, custody compliance, multi-jurisdictional regulatory requirements) and C = 180 (a handful of approved operators globally, restricted transport options, limited market access). The balance score for this phase is 0.32 out of 1.0. It runs at approximately 21% of its structural potential.

docs.title: Check 2: Phase-to-phase coherence (40% of the score)
docs.text:
For each boundary between adjacent phases, the coherence score is:

$$\Phi_j = 1 - \left|\frac{\ln(r_j / \varphi)}{\ln(\varphi)}\right|, \quad r_j = \frac{N_{j+1}}{N_j}$$

When $r_j$ equals $\varphi$, the score is 1. The further $r_j$ deviates from $\varphi$ in either direction, the lower the score. The coherence score for the chain is the average across all boundaries.

docs.title: Check 3: Operational efficiency (20% of the score)
docs.text:
For each phase, the efficiency score measures how close the phase runs to its structural potential:

$$S_i = \frac{4 \cdot D_i \cdot C_i}{(D_i + C_i)^2}$$

This score is maximised at 1 when D and C are equal, and falls toward 0 as they diverge in either direction. It is structurally related to the balance score but captures the capacity utilisation directly: a phase running at low efficiency is wasting the resources it consumes.

docs.title: The composite score
docs.text: $$\text{TVPCI} = 0.4 \cdot \bar{B} + 0.4 \cdot \bar{\Phi} + 0.2 \cdot \bar{S}$$

docs.title: The opacity correction
docs.text:
Some phases cannot be assessed because the data is not available: private contracts, informal trade, commercially sensitive logistics, or government-restricted information. For every opaque phase, the score is reduced by up to 15%. This is not a penalty for wrongdoing. It is a structural acknowledgement that a chain we cannot fully see cannot be given a high trust score, because the hidden phases may be the weakest ones.

$$\text{TVPCI}{\text{adj}} = \text{TVPCI} \times \left(1 - 0.15 \times \frac{P{\text{opaque}}}{P_{\text{total}}}\right)$$

The opacity of Phase 6 in the gold chain (vaulting) is a structural property of that phase, not a deliberate concealment. Vault contents are confidential for legal and security reasons. The TVPCI records this as a constraint on the confidence of that phase's contribution to the score, not as evidence of misconduct.

docs.title: What the Score Means
docs.text: Score Label Interpretation 90-100 Structurally coherent The price reflects the chain; high trust 75-89 Near convergence Minor structural issues; mostly reliable 55-74 Moderate divergence Specific phases are distorting the price 35-54 Significant divergence The price obscures major structural problems 0-34 Critical divergence The market price and true value are largely disconnected

docs.title: Two Real Chains
docs.text:
Gold: The gold supply chain spans eight phases from geological occurrence to exchange registration. The terminal end (exchange) is among the most transparent commodity markets in the world. The upstream end (geology, extraction, processing) is physically intensive and commercially private. Phase 6 (vaulting and logistics) is structurally the weakest link: low balance score, severe $\varphi$ boundary suppression, and partial opacity. These factors combine to produce a TVPCI well below the "near convergence" range, despite the terminal price being highly efficient in the financial sense. The price is reliable as a market signal. It is not reliable as a structural signal.

Shea: The shea butter chain runs from West African collectors to European retail. Farmgate price is approximately \$150 per tonne. European retail equivalent is \$47,500 per tonne. The 317x amplification is heavily concentrated at the European processing and retail end. The collector phase has few market connections, many imposed constraints, and limited access to price information or alternative buyers. The $\varphi$ boundary scores between the collector and export phases are very low. Informal flows between collection and export are largely opaque, applying an additional opacity correction. The shea chain's TVPCI reflects this: a market price that tells you a great deal about European retail economics and very little about the structural state of the chain at origin.

docs.title: The Core Idea
docs.text:
The TVPCI is a structural audit of a supply chain's prices. It does not say what a price should be. It says how well the current price reflects the structural state of the chain that produced the good: how balanced the phases are, whether value passes between them in natural proportion, whether the value cycle closes, who captures each step of amplification, and how fragile the chain is to disruption.

A high TVPCI means the market price and true value are close together. A low TVPCI means they are far apart, and somewhere in the chain, structural conditions are preventing value from reaching the people and places that created it.

The score makes that gap visible, measurable, and specific enough to act on.

Document: TVPCI Explained Simply Version: 2.1, April 2026 Part of the TrueValue Analytics framework documentation

docs.title: Technical Specification and Methodology
docs.text: Version: 1.0 Status: Specification Applies to: Gold supply chain (Phase 0–7), Shea supply chain (Phase 0–6) Framework: TrueValue Analytics — C-G-N TrueValue model

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
The True Value Pricing Convergence Index (TVPCI) is a dimensionless composite index, ranging from 0 to 100, that measures how closely the structural condition of a supply chain would allow an observed market price to converge toward its True Value.

It does not produce a price. It produces a structural reading — a quantitative measure of how much friction, imbalance, and incoherence exists within the physical chain that would cause market price to diverge from True Value. When TVPCI = 100, the chain is operating at maximum structural integrity: value flows proportionally through every phase, all phases are internally balanced, and the chain imposes no structural distortion on price. As TVPCI falls, the gap between market price and True Value is structurally explained — not by speculation or intent, but by measurable phase-level C-G-N conditions.

This index is the primary quantitative output of the TrueValue Analytics platform. It precedes financial analysis; it does not replace it.

docs.title: 2. Position in the Analytical Stack
docs.text:
Layer 1 — Physical Supply Chain        (Phases 0–N, C-G-N metrics per phase)
Layer 2 — Value Chain                  (Phase-aligned costs, margins, prices)
Layer 3 — TVPCI                        (Composite structural integrity score)
Layer 4 — True Value Pricing           (Price convergence interpretation)
Layer 5 — Financial Abstraction        (Paper claims, leverage — OUT OF SCOPE here)

The TVPCI sits at Layer 3. It is computed entirely from Layers 1–2 inputs and feeds forward into Layer 4. It must never be computed from Layer 5 data (paper gold, financial derivatives, exchange positioning).

docs.title: 3.1 C-G-N Phase State
docs.text:
Each supply chain phase (i) is characterised by three quantities computed by the Tholonic engine:

Definition total (sum of constraint parameters, 0–100 each):

$$D_i = \sum_{k} d_{i,k}$$

Contribution total (sum of integration parameters, 0–100 each):

$$C_i = \sum_{k} c_{i,k}$$

Balance score (0–100, maximum when (D_i = C_i)):

$$B_i = 100 \cdot \exp!\left(-2 \cdot \frac{|D_i - C_i|}{\max(D_i, C_i)}\right)$$

Sustainability index (higher is more efficient):

$$S_i = \frac{100}{|D_i - C_i|^2 + E_{\text{base}}} \qquad E_{\text{base}} = 10$$

N-state (emergent operational capacity):

$$N_i = \sqrt{D_i \cdot C_i} \cdot \frac{B_i}{100}$$

docs.title: 3.2 Phase Boundary Coherence (φ-model)
docs.text:
Between adjacent phases, the ratio of N-states is compared to the golden ratio (\varphi = 1.61803\ldots):

$$r_{i \to i+1} = \frac{N_{i+1}}{N_i}$$

Boundary φ-score (100 when (r = \varphi), decaying exponentially away from it):

$$\Phi_{i \to i+1} = 100 \cdot \exp!\left(-2 \cdot \frac{|r_{i \to i+1} - \varphi|}{\varphi}\right)$$

When (r \ll \varphi): value is suppressed at the boundary (retained upstream or extracted by an intermediary). When (r \gg \varphi): disproportionate recovery — structurally unstable, typically precedes a collapse. When (r \approx \varphi): value passes through in natural proportion — no structural distortion at this boundary.

Why φ? — Mathematical justification

The N-state is a geometric mean ((N_i = \sqrt{D_i \cdot C_i})), so the question arises: why should the ratio of consecutive N-states converge to φ, a constant that classically emerges from additive (Fibonacci-type) recursion, not from geometric means?

The answer lies in the Tholonic propagation rule. When the D and C parameters of successive phases follow the Fibonacci inheritance pattern — each phase's D receiving the prior phase's N-value, and each phase's C receiving the prior phase's D-value — the D and C sequences become consecutive Fibonacci numbers. Substituting (D_n = F_{n+1}) and (C_n = F_n):

$$\frac{N_{n+1}}{N_n} = \frac{\sqrt{F_{n+2} \cdot F_{n+1}}}{\sqrt{F_{n+1} \cdot F_n}} = \sqrt{\frac{F_{n+2}}{F_n}}$$

Using the Fibonacci identity (F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n):

$$\frac{F_{n+2}}{F_n} = \frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n} + 1 \;\xrightarrow{n \to \infty}\; \varphi + 1 = \varphi^2$$

Therefore:

$$\frac{N_{n+1}}{N_n} \;\to\; \sqrt{\varphi^2} = \varphi$$

The φ-benchmark is not arbitrary. It measures the structural fidelity of the underlying D and C parameters to the Fibonacci propagation pattern that the Tholonic framework generates from first principles. A boundary ratio at φ indicates that the phase's D and C parameters are inheriting value from the prior phase in the natural Tholonic proportion. Deviation from φ is a quantitative signal that this proportional inheritance has been disrupted — by extraction, suppression, or imbalance.

docs.title: 3.3 Chain-Level Aggregates
docs.text:
Mean phase balance across (P) phases:

$$\bar{B} = \frac{1}{P} \sum_{i=0}^{P-1} B_i$$

Mean phase sustainability:

$$\bar{S}{\text{norm}} = \frac{\bar{S} - S{\min}}{S_{\max} - S_{\min}} \cdot 100 \qquad \text{(normalised to 0–100)}$$

System φ-coherence across (P-1) boundaries:

$$\bar{\Phi} = \frac{1}{P-1} \sum_{i=0}^{P-2} \Phi_{i \to i+1}$$

docs.title: 4. TVPCI Composite Formula
docs.text:
The TVPCI is a weighted composite of three structural sub-scores:

$$\text{TVPCI} = w_B \cdot \bar{B} + w_\Phi \cdot \bar{\Phi} + w_S \cdot \bar{S}_{\text{norm}}$$

docs.title: 4.1 Default Weights
docs.text:
Sub-score Symbol Default Weight Rationale Phase Balance (\bar{B}) 0.40 D-C balance is the primary sustainability condition Boundary Coherence (\bar{\Phi}) 0.40 φ-proportionality determines value flow integrity Phase Sustainability (\bar{S}_{\text{norm}}) 0.20 Energy cost of imbalance; partially captured by (\bar{B})

Weights must sum to 1.0. Commodity-specific weight profiles may be defined (see Section 7).

docs.title: 4.2 Opacity Correction Factor
docs.text:
Phases with data_quality: "OPAQUE" introduce structural uncertainty. For each opaque phase (j), the sub-scores contributed by phase (j) are replaced by the chain mean of the transparent phases, and a transparency penalty is applied:

$$\text{TVPCI}{\text{adjusted}} = \text{TVPCI} \cdot \left(1 - \alpha \cdot \frac{N{\text{opaque}}}{P}\right)$$

Where: - (\alpha = 0.15): maximum per-opaque-phase penalty (15%) - (N_{\text{opaque}}): number of phases flagged OPAQUE - (P): total phases

This penalty is not punitive. It is the structural consequence of incomplete information: a chain with opaque phases cannot be verified as operating at its stated TVPCI.

docs.title: 5.1 Phase Balance ((\bar{B}))
docs.text: Score Condition Interpretation 95–100 Near-perfect D-C balance All phases operating near structural optimum 80–94 Good balance Minor phase-level imbalances; chain broadly healthy 60–79 Fair balance One or more phases with meaningful D-C friction 40–59 Poor balance Multiple phases under-performing; value loss visible 0–39 Critical imbalance Chain-wide structural failure; pricing signal unreliable

docs.title: 5.2 Boundary Coherence ((\bar{\Phi}))
docs.text: Score Ratio Profile Interpretation 80–100 (r \approx \varphi) across most boundaries Value passes proportionally — no structural extraction 55–79 Mild deviation Localised boundary failures; monitor identified phases 35–54 Moderate deviation Systematic proportionality breakdown; value capture likely 0–34 Severe deviation Chain-wide incoherence; market price structurally divorced from True Value

docs.title: 5.3 Composite TVPCI
docs.text: TVPCI Label Pricing Interpretation 90–100 Structurally Coherent Market price and True Value structurally aligned; convergence expected 75–89 Near Convergence Minor structural friction; small but measurable price divergence 55–74 Moderate Divergence Identifiable phases distorting price; True Value partially obscured 35–54 Significant Divergence Structural price distortion; financial analysis will overstate or understate value 0–34 Critical Divergence Market price does not reflect physical chain conditions; True Value inaccessible from price alone

docs.title: 6. Phase-Level TVPCI Contribution
docs.text:
Each phase's contribution to the overall TVPCI can be decomposed to identify which phases are suppressing chain-wide convergence. The phase TVPCI contribution is:

$$\text{TVPCI}i = \frac{w_B \cdot B_i + w_S \cdot S{i,\text{norm}}}{P} + \frac{w_\Phi \cdot (\Phi_{i-1 \to i} + \Phi_{i \to i+1})}{2(P-1)}$$

(Boundary terms use single-side values for terminal phases.)

This decomposition supports the bottleneck identification use case: the phase with the lowest (\text{TVPCI}_i) is the point where structural intervention would produce the largest gain in chain-wide convergence.

docs.title: 7.1 Gold (Phases 0–7)
docs.text:
Known structural characteristics:

  • Phase 6 (Vaulting) is the system's weakest phase: high D (security, compliance), low C (vault network, transport flexibility), balance target 0.50.
  • Phase 7 (COMEX registration) is the most transparent: regulatory framework enforces balance, balance target 0.85.

docs.title: 8. Relationship to True Value Price
docs.text:
The TVPCI does not produce a price. It produces the structural condition under which a price can be interpreted. The relationship is:

$$P_{\text{market}} = P_{\text{true}} \cdot \left(1 + \delta_{\text{structural}}\right)$$

Where (\delta_{\text{structural}}) is a signed divergence term. The TVPCI provides the magnitude of (|\delta_{\text{structural}}|) in structural terms:

$$|\delta_{\text{structural}}| \propto \left(1 - \frac{\text{TVPCI}}{100}\right)$$

A TVPCI of 80 does not mean the market price is 20% wrong. It means that 20 structural index points of friction, imbalance, and incoherence exist within the chain — and that any price formed in that chain carries a structurally unexplained component of that magnitude. Whether that component manifests as overpricing, underpricing, or redistribution between chain participants is a question for Layer 4 (True Value Pricing) and Layer 5 analysis.
